title: Connectome spiking-model responses to up to 10 fly head sensory neurons agree less between FlyWire and BANC than between brain sides; gain, sign and nerve-cord changes do not close the gap
abstract: Question: does a whole-brain connectome spiking model give the same prediction when it is built from a second fly? Approach: we re-implemented the Shiu et al. 2024 leaky integrate-and-fire model (validated against the original Brian2 code, neuron-level log-rate r = 0.993) and built it from FlyWire v783 and BANC v888. We activated up to 10 neurons of each of 89 shared head sensory cell types on each side and compared the responses of 7,930 matched cell types. Results: 105 of 114 antennal-lobe stimulus sides ignite one global state (about 8,500 neurons) that is almost the same for every stimulus (Jaccard 0.98 between stimuli). For sparse responses (mechanosensory, gustatory and other inputs), the share of active cell types common to two runs was 0.92 for trial halves, 0.54 after a synapse-count noise model, 0.67 for other seed neurons, 0.27 for left vs right side of one map, and 0.11 between FlyWire and BANC (hemisphere vs between maps p = 3.6e-5, 30 stimuli). A size-matched metric and descending-neuron outputs gave the same order. A BANC gain of 1.34 or 1.79, FlyWire transmitter signs, or removal of the nerve cord did not increase agreement. A threshold-free linear model gave the same order (0.72, 0.41, 0.25), and agreement between maps fell from 0.27 at the first synapse to 0.03 at two synapses. Conclusion: with published parameters, model predictions beyond the first-order targets are specific to the map. Limitations: model results only, no comparison with measured activity; two female flies with different reconstruction pipelines, so biological and technical differences are not separated; 10-neuron seed sets give weak drive.
